nodes.title: Don't tightly couple FSDP checkpoint_wrapper in auto_wrap_policy

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Current checkpoint_wrapper: requires manual wrap of FSDP module, i.e. first the module is wrapped with the checkpoint wrapper, and then FSDP wrapper is used.
Although, frequently users don't have access to the model code and can't insert wrappers on submodules and thus use FSDP's auto_wrap_policy to automatically nest FSDP instances. Since auto_wrap currently does not support adding checkpoint_wrappers to the module, this means that checkpoint_wrapper + auto_wrap cannot be used effectively.
To fix this, we can add a checkpoint=False argument to FSDP constructor, and pass this into auto_wrapping. This will ensure that modules can be wrapped with checkpointing during auto_wrap.
A downside of this approach would be that activation checkpointed modules would be tightly coupled to FSDP-wrapped modules, because it would only be wrapped with the auto wrap policy decides to wrap an FSDP module. Although ideally, the optimal setup might be some sort of a solution where we might decide to wrap an FSDP module without checkpointing, or wrap a module with checkpointing but not FSDP. This can be taken as a follow up work.

t = torch.tensor([1., 2.], requires_grad=True, device=torch.device("cuda"))
t.register_hook(hook_with_callback)
output = t ** 2
loss = output.sum()
loss.backward()

🐛 Describe the bug
Description
Usually, when applying torch.unique to a specific dimension, torch.unique(dim=x) returns output that, except for dim x, matches the size of the input tensor.
However, in the case where dim x in the input tensor has length zero, the input dimensions are discarded, and torch.unique output erroneously has size [0]. This happens regardless of the shape of the input tensor.
Steps to reproduce:
import torch

# Create a multi-dimensional tensor, with a single zero-length dimension.
input_tensor = torch.randint(3, [0, 4])

# Call `torch.unique` on the tensor, along the zero-length dimension.
input_tensor.unique(dim=0)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], dtype=torch.int64)
Expected behaviour
Except for the dimension supplied to dim, the dimensions of the output of unique should always match the input.
torch.randint(3, [0, 4]).unique(dim=0)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], size=(0, 4), dtype=torch.int64)




# Or, for a differently-sized input tensor:
torch.randint(3, [2, 0, 9]).unique(dim=1)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], size=(2, 0, 9), dtype=torch.int64)
Actual behaviour
Calling torch.unique(dim=x), where x is a zero-length dimension, returns a tensor of size [0], regardless of any other dimensions of the input tensor.
torch.randint(3, [0, 4]).unique(dim=0)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], dtype=torch.int64)




torch.randint(3, [2, 0, 9]).unique(dim=1)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], dtype=torch.int64)
Why do I expect the behaviour in "Expected behaviour"?
When acting along a zero-length dimension, other Pytorch methods preserve the dimensions of the input tensor, rather than returning a tensor of size [0].
Such as sort:
import torch

# Create a multi-dimensional tensor, with a single zero-length dimension.
input_tensor = torch.randint(3, [0, 4])

# Call `torch.sort` on the tensor, along the zero-length dimension.
input_tensor.sort(dim=0).values

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], size=(0, 4), dtype=torch.int64)
And cat:
import torch

# Create a multi-dimensional tensor, with a single zero-length dimension.
input_tensor = torch.randint(3, [0, 4])

# Call `torch.sort` on the tensor, along the zero-length dimension.
torch.cat([input_tensor]*2, dim=0)

# Output:
# torch.tensor([], size=(0, 4), dtype=torch.int64)
Proposed changes


Replace {0} on this line with sizes

if not self._qkv_same_embed_dim:

Some DDP comms hook, like PowetSGD, are stateful and must be part of model checkpointing to enable trainer restarts.

nodes.bodyText:
Standard JIT design has compilation run off-thread, so that normal user code can continue running while compilation is still occurring. Unfortunately, torchdynamo's implementation in Python makes this difficult to do, as in standard Python there is a GIL which prevents useful parallelization of Python work. This means that we need to think about our off main thread strategy earlier rather than later, as it may imply architectural changes that are easier to do earlier in this project's lifetime.
I can imagine a number of possible ways to skin this cat:

Put torchdynamo evaluation in a separate process
Put torchdynamo in a subinterpreter in the same process

All strategies involving a separate Python interpreter will have to somehow transmit all of the frame information as well as locals for evaluation


Rewrite torchdynamo in C++ (ugh)
Rewrite torchdynamo in RPython
Do nothing and pray the host program spends enough time in PyTorch operations that we can make useful progress with standard threading
Do nothing for symbolic evaluation, but offload FX graph compilation to another thread

It would be good to know the PoR here.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import pytorch_lightning as pl

class MovieLensDummyDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):

        self.items = torch.randint(0,n_users,(n,)).type(torch.int32)
        self.labels = torch.randint(0,2,(n,)).type(torch.uint8)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return self.users[idx], self.items[idx], self.labels[idx]

    def __len__(self):
        return self.users.shape[0]


class NCF(pl.LightningModule):
    """ Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF)
    
        Args:
            num_users (int): Number of unique users
            num_items (int): Number of unique items
            ratings (pd.DataFrame): Dataframe containing the movie ratings for training
            all_movieIds (list): List containing all movieIds (train + test)

        self.user_embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=num_users, embedding_dim=8)
        self.item_embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=num_items, embedding_dim=8)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=16, out_features=64)
        self.fc1_activation = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=64, out_features=32)

        vector = torch.cat([user_embedded, item_embedded], dim=-1)

        # Pass through dense layer
        vector = self.fc1_activation(self.fc1(vector))
        vector = self.fc2_activation(self.fc2(vector))

        # Output layer

    def training_step(self, batch, batch_idx):

🐛 Describe the bug
Torch functions which can be represented by ConstantOfShape op are expanded to Constant op. This happens even with do_constant_folding=False. Here is an example script:
import os

import onnx
import torch


class OnesLike(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + torch.ones_like(x)


# torch 1.10 or later cannot export this if we change 100 to 1000.
x = torch.ones(100, 1000, 1000)
torch.onnx.export(OnesLike(), x, 'ones_like.onnx',
                  do_constant_folding=False,
                  opset_version=13)

m = onnx.load("ones_like.onnx")

# 1.9: ['Shape', 'ConstantOfShape', 'Add'] 210
# 1.10: ['Constant', 'Add'] 400000191
# 1.11: ['Constant', 'Add'] 400000233
print([n.op_type for n in m.graph.node], os.stat("ones_like.onnx").st_size)
With torch 1.9, it output ['Shape', 'ConstantOfShape', 'Add'] 210 but with 1.10 and 1.11, it output ['Constant', 'Add'] 400000XXX.
Even worse, this may make ONNX export fail due to the 2GB limit of protobuf. It seems torch.onnx does not use DataLocation.EXTERNAL of onnx::TensorProto for Constant op, so exporting stops working if we change 100, 1000, 1000 in the above script to 1000, 1000, 1000.
In general, I think it is better to try using ConstantOfShape instead of Constant when a Constant seems to have the same value. It'd be also a good idea not to apply constant folding for large tensors, especially when do_constant_folding is False.

This is a bitfield that is concurrently accesses and modified. Concurrent bitfield modification is UD.

background thread calls TensorImpl::set_size

📚 The doc issue
The ONNX related documentation, in particular the subsection of tracing vs scripting, mentions an argument that has been removed in version 1.11.
Concretely, in the 'Scripting' part:

Call torch.onnx.export() with the ScriptModule as the model, and set the example_outputs arg. This is required so that the types and shapes of the outputs can be captured without executing the model.

However, the example_outputs arg has been removed entirely, as it appears that the model is now executed internally, in order to retrieve the example outputs:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/onnx/utils.py
    
    
         Line 470
      in
      9905b1f
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def _get_example_outputs(model, args): 
        
    
  


Coming from here: 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/onnx/utils.py
    
    
         Line 559
      in
      9905b1f
    
  
  
    

        
          
           example_outputs = _get_example_outputs(model, args) 
        
    
  


Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Replace

Call torch.onnx.export() with the ScriptModule as the model, and set the example_outputs arg. This is required so that the types and shapes of the outputs can be captured without executing the model.

by

Call torch.onnx.export() with the ScriptModule as the model. The args are still required, but they will be used internally only to produce example outputs, so that the types and shapes of the outputs can be captured. No tracing will be performed.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Mixed precision training for FSDP recently landed: #75024, however, it does not work out of the box for batch norm at the moment.
If mixed precision is attempted to be used with batchnorm/syncbatchnorm, an error similar to the below is encountered:
>>> z = torch.ones(128, 128, 128).to(torch.float16)
>>> x = nn.BatchNorm1d(128)
>>> x(z)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 1110, in _call_impl
    return forward_call(*input, **kwargs)
  File "/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/batchnorm.py", line 179, in forward
    self.eps,
  File "/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/functional.py", line 2399, in batch_norm
    input, weight, bias, running_mean, running_var, training, momentum, eps, torch.backends.cudnn.enabled
RuntimeError: "batch_norm" not implemented for 'Half'

In general, even if the rest of the model (i.e. dense layers) are using mixed precision, we want to disable mixed precision for BN layers. In general, fp32 full precision computation is recommended for batchnorm, via resources such as https://nvidia.github.io/apex/amp.html.
The proposal here is to force disabling of mixed precision of BN layers, even if user specifies mixed precision for them. If we are wrapping a batchnorm instance in constructor, we simply add an isinstance check in constructor, and disable mixed precision if we are in batchnorm.
We'd want to ensure that this works for both ways to wrap FSDP: enable_wrap + wrap, as well as auto_wrap_policy.
As a follow up change, we can also support forcing inputs to fp32 prior to being run in a batchnorm.
To test, we can add unittests to test_fsdp_mixed_precision as well as run ResNet internal benchmark to validate that the change works.
It remains an open issue on how to resolve this for modules that contain batchnorm as a submodule, but user wraps these modules instead of just the batchnorm instance. Possibly we will not support this in the near term and document as so.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Not easily knowing when something is fused has bitten the e3nn team quite a bit I think. Turns out control flow prevented all their ridiculously fuseable code from being fully optimized. Removing control flow shows significant increase in perf (4x to 7x).
Another example is a recent feature request #75251 . The fusers (both nnc(assume this is default) and nvfuser) makes it trivial to try this implementation and gives much better performance, but I don't know whether they actually fully fused the code. In particular, when I replaced square with pow(x, 2) I got a significant speedup.
Can we have a context in which a call to torch.jit.script fails if it wasn't able to entirely fuse it?
Example
with torch.jit.fuser("fuser2", force_fusion=True):
    fused_op = torch.jit.script(op)

Alternatives
There are options to inspect whether a fusion succeeded or not via environment variable, inspecting the result of torch.jit.script, etc. However, this seems pretty difficult for most users to give us good feedback on whether it worked on their case and open issues if it didn't. Surely we'd want to know when fusion failed to collect snippets or user requests.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Right now FSDP assumes module execution order is the same across ranks without validation. This is not safe, it would either result in hang or incorrect results.
Propose to add validation in the following way, alternative ways are welcomed. Note the following approach will work efficiently for graphs whose execution order do not change over iterations. If graph execution order changes after 1st iteration, it still can validate execution orders are the same across ranks, but that will be expensive, so we can chose to give users a warning like "graph execution orders are changed but they are not validated to be the same across ranks, it has risk to result in training hang or incorrect results".
The proposal assumes each rank wraps the same module in the same way:

During the first iteration, if module is the root, traverse all the children fsdp modules, and assign each fsdp module a id. e.g., fsdp_module1.id = traverse_index.
In current fsdp implementation, root fsdp module keeps a list called "_fsdp_graph_order" to maintain the fsdp module references in the execution order. We can have a new list to put the active fsdp module's id "fsdp_module.id" into it, and trace the executed fsdp modules using the ids for both forward and backward pass . then at the end of backward pass, the new list will capture the execution order of fsdp modules for the first iteration. we can broadcast rank 0's execution order list to other ranks and let each rank check whether the execution order list matches or not. if not, throw errors.
after 1st iteration, we can continue to trace the fsdp module execution orders using the ids, and check whether it is the same as the one captured in the first iteration. If the order changed after 1st iteration, give users a warning

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Today, PyTorch offers a few private hooks for state_dict and load_state_dict that exist to allow users to run post and pre processing respectively when saving and loading model checkpoints.
Current state_dict post hook: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L1265
Current state_dict pre hook: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L1408
This proposal seeks to:

Propose 2 new hooks so that state_dict and load_state_dict both have pre and post hooks
Aim to consolidate all of the 4 hooks and make their semantics consistent
Provide a vision where all 4 new APIs are public and can be used by PyTorch users in a stable fashion.

Current State

_register_state_dict_hook allows registration of a Callable[self, state_dict, prefix, local_metadata] -> Optional[Dict[str, Tensor]] and is run after the state_dict of self (and all of its children) is processed. It can modify state_dict and optionally return a new one.
_register_load_state_dict_pre_hook allows registration of a Callable[state_dict, prefix, local_metadatra, missing_keys, unexpected_keys, error_msgs] or a Callable[self, state_dict, prefix, local_metadatra, missing_keys, unexpected_keys, error_msgs] if with_module=True], and is run before loading state dict into self (and all of its children).

Proposed State
Revamped existing APIs:

register_state_dict_post_hook -> Same as (1) above, but we've renamed it to clearly indicate this is a post hook. This is a bit inconsistent with nn.Module register_hook semantics, but arguably more clear and will be consistent with state_dict hook APIs, which should be enough for consistency. This hook will behave in the same way it currently does.
register_load_state_dict_pre_hook -> Same as (2) above, but we will remove with_module argument and always provide the self module into the API. Users can simply ignore this module in their function if needed. EDIT (@janeyx99): We should also allow the hook to optionally return a new state_dict, if desired, as it will cover the use case where one may want to completely change up the state_dict. Relevant PR #105953 where we have this for the optimizer.

New APIs:

register_state_dict_pre_hook: Callable[self, prefix] -> None which is a state_dict() pre hook that will be run before the state_dict is computed for self (and all of its children). We do not pass in the destination argument is it is deprecated into this hook.
register_load_state_dict_post_hook: Callable[self] -> None which is a load_state_dict() post hook that runs after state dict is loaded into self module and all of its children. Note that this is consistent with the rest of the APIs - hooks are called either before or after self computation and all children computation has taken place, never in between. Another proposal is that the hook can be a Callable[self, NamedTuple] -> NamedTuple where the NamedTuple contains the missing_keys and unexpected_keys that was returned by load_state_dict, and the user can do some optional processing / addition / removal and return a new NamedTuple. Although, we are not aware of any use case requiring that at the moment, so suggesting to keep it simple for now.
Similar to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/module.py#L1389, we should offer a _register_load_state_dict_post_hook that is called after load_state_dict for a particular nn.Module is completed.

The goal is to have this hook called even for modules that aren't at the top level during load_state_dict; and this hook should be called after self module is loaded as well as all of self's children.
In addition, similar to load_state_dict's existing pre-hook, state_dict should also offer a pre-hook for any module-specific preprocessing that modules may want to run before calling into state_dict.  This can be invoked before the call to self._state_dict_impl. API to register this could be _register_state_dict_pre_hook. Unfortunately, the current state_dict hook is a post hook but is named _register_state_dict_hook which is a bit unclear as to whether it is a pre/post hook. Since the API is private, we could consider refactoring _register_state_dict_hook to _register_state_dict_post_hook.
Plan moving forward
Since these are all public facing APIs, we can add them in addition to the old existing hooks and keep the old ones for legacy reasons and add deprecated warnings.
Motivating use case:

FullyShardedDataParallel in particular needs register_load_state_dict_post_hook and register_load_state_dict_pre_hook to enter/exit the full parameter summoning context. We don't want to do this in load_state_dict itself since load_state_dict is not overridable (it won't be called for submodules). Draft PR:

cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki @kshitij12345 @saketh-are

🐛 Describe the bug
torch.multiprocessing does not propagate global state like the default dtype to worker processes when using the forkserver start method:
import torch
from torch import multiprocessing as mp


def func(i):
    print(f"{i}: {torch.get_default_dtype()}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
    ctx = mp.get_context("forkserver")
    with ctx.Pool() as p:
        p.map(func, range(3))

    print("done")
gives
$ python torch-mp.py 
0: torch.float32
1: torch.float32
2: torch.float32
done

on 1.11 and 1.10. If you change it to fork, all of them print float64. This leads to dtype errors when the tensors are brought back to the parent process.
Since switching to forkserver (necessary for CUDA, and in my experience also on many systems where fork leads to hangs because of some kind of OpenMP issue) should not have this problem...
Is there a way to load/restore PyTorch's global settings? Obviously I can manually pass the default dtype to the worker process, but ideally I'd like to use something more general and forward compatible.
Versions

CUDA
Ubuntu

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Sometimes, FSDP wraps models with components such as model parallelism modules, and users would like to ignore these parameters / modules when wrapping their overall model with FSDP.
This is similar to DDP which offers the following API to do so: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/parallel/distributed.py#L1698
In order to implement this in FSDP, we can do the following:

Add an argument params_to_ignore or modules_to_ignore which will specify the modules that should not be wrapped in FSDP at all, to ensure that these parameters / modules will not be sharded at all.
Implement this by skipping these parameters when constructing FlatParameter: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/fsdp/fully_sharded_data_parallel.py#L343
Bypass these parameters explicitly during state_dict / load_state_dict pre and post processing.

As a result, FSDP will not be aware of these parameters.
